newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook - Prices seen firming in longer term.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook - Prices seen firming in longer term.

text.p: Soft commodity prices could turn higher in the longer term, but the real key for market sentiment will come from fundamental factors, traders said on Monday.
New York's equivalent futures markets were likely to set the tone for London as fund players reacted to the gyrations of the supply-demand equation, they said.
In cocoa, traders said the outlook was still mixed although market prices could rise on more bullish fundamental factors.
On Friday, U.S. first-quarter cocoa grinds jumped by 20.74 percent from year-ago levels, sharply higher than forecasts for flat to five percent higher.
Robin Edwards, managing director of Sabre Fund Management, said cocoa should consolidate for the next few weeks, with July lingering between 950 and 1,050 stg.

But within two to three months, he expected cocoa to finally break out of its recent range to the upside. An expected pick-up in European economic growth should boost demand for cocoa products, he said.
Traders said fund buying should emerge when London's July contract closes in on this month's 1,065 stg peak, further bolstering cocoa prices.
But others were less convinced, noting that CSCE July cocoa has tested and failed to pierce resistance at a gap between $1,480 and $1,501.
Fundamentally, traders will continue to look for hints as to the size and quality of the Ivorian crop.

On Friday local exporters and crop analysts said cocoa arrivals at Ivorian ports of Ivory Coast 1996/97 main crop totalled 970-980,000 tonnes by mid-April, close to the record last season. The main crop last season reached just over one million tonnes.
Robusta coffee futures, fuelled by New York's recent rally, are slowly turning higher after a consolidative phase but traders say the picture is far from bullish.

Technical analysts said London's July contract could challenge $1,700 and then $1,730, with support seen safe at just above $1,600, but it still faces an uphill struggle to regain a foothold above $1,820.
In the longer term, the market will keep a close watch on weather news from Brazil as the frost season gets underway from late May or early June.
While New York forges ahead, the well-supplied robustas market is struggling to keep pace while arabicas futures trade at a record of more than 60 percent over robusta prices.

Traders said arrivals from the main Indonesian harvest were pressuring the London market and while the crop is expected to be less than last year, it is still relatively good compared with some recent seasons.
But demand from roasters -- especially in Europe -- is flimsy with manufacturers holding comfortable stocks and in no hurry to make extra purchases.
In sugar, London is expected to drift in ranges while the battle between trade and fund players in New York plays itself out before the May raws contract expires.
"It's hard to forecast what London will do," said one trader. "August/October widened with the rolling into August prior to the May expiry and it might slide down in the next few days."
Nearby spreads have reverted to their normal backwardation down the futures board but traders said the market still needed time to stabilise after the gyrations wreaked by last week's whites expiry.
"You've just had an expiry of the spot month and it always takes around two or three weeks for the market to establish itself once again," said another trader.
Despite the rangebound activity seen in London last week, emerging physical offtake could provide some support to the market, traders said,
